title: What Causes High Humidity in a House?
h1: What Causes High Humidity in a House, and How Can You Lower It?
description: High indoor humidity usually comes from daily activities, coastal air, poor ventilation or an AC that isn't removing moisture. Here's how to find and fix it.
quick_answer: High indoor humidity usually comes from moisture you create inside, like showers, cooking and laundry, combined with poor ventilation. Damp coastal air, leaks, a crawl space and an air conditioner that short cycles or runs the fan nonstop can add to it. Most homes stay comfortable between about 30 and 50 percent humidity.
body:
A house that feels sticky, smells musty or fogs up its windows has more moisture in the air than it can get rid of. Along the coast, the marine layer adds to the problem, but the source is often inside the home. Finding where the moisture comes from is the first step to fixing it.

What everyday activities add moisture?

A family puts a lot of water into the air without noticing:

  • Hot showers and baths, especially without an exhaust fan running
  • Cooking, boiling water and running a dishwasher
  • Drying clothes on racks indoors
  • Houseplants, aquariums and indoor pets
  • Mopping floors and cleaning with water

None of these is a problem on its own. Trouble starts when the moisture has no way out.

How does ventilation affect humidity?

Newer windows and weatherstripping keep drafts out, but they also keep moisture in. Bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans are meant to remove humid air at the source. If the fan is weak, noisy or vents into the attic instead of outside, the moisture stays.

Check your laundry setup too. A dryer vent that has come loose behind the dryer, or one that's crushed or clogged, can push warm, wet air into the laundry room or garage.

Can my air conditioner cause high humidity?

Yes. Your AC removes moisture as it cools, but only when it runs properly. A few common issues get in the way:

  • Oversized system. A unit that's too big cools the house fast and shuts off before it has time to pull moisture out. The house feels cold and clammy.
  • Fan set to ON. When the blower runs constantly, water on the cold coil can evaporate back into the house between cooling cycles. Setting the fan to AUTO usually helps.
  • Dirty coil or low airflow. Poor airflow and dirty coils reduce how well the system dries the air.
  • Leaky return ducts. Return ducts in an attic or crawl space can pull in damp outside air if they leak.

Mild coastal weather plays a role as well. On cool, foggy days the AC may not run at all, so nothing is drying the air.

What hidden sources should you look for?

If the obvious causes are covered and the house still feels damp, look for:

  1. Slow plumbing leaks under sinks or behind walls
  2. Roof or window leaks after rain
  3. A damp crawl space under a raised foundation
  4. Sprinklers spraying against stucco walls
  5. A clogged AC condensate drain backing up water
  6. Poor grading that sends water toward the foundation

Why does the coast make humidity worse?

Homes near the ocean deal with the marine layer, which brings fog and damp air inland on many mornings, especially in late spring and early summer. Windows left open on those days let that moisture straight in.

Inland homes usually see drier outdoor air, but humidity can still build up inside from showers, cooking and a poorly ventilated laundry room.

What are the signs of too much humidity?

  • Condensation on windows, especially in the morning
  • A musty smell in closets or bathrooms
  • Mold or mildew in shower corners, window frames or on ceilings
  • Peeling paint or bubbling wallpaper
  • Bedding, towels and clothes that feel damp
  • Allergy symptoms that get worse at home

An inexpensive hygrometer from a hardware store tells you the actual number. Readings that stay above about 50 to 60 percent mean it's time to act.

How do you lower indoor humidity?

Start with the simple fixes, then move to equipment if needed:

  1. Run bathroom fans during showers and for a while after.
  2. Use the range hood when cooking, and make sure it vents outside.
  3. Dry laundry in a properly vented dryer.
  4. Set the thermostat fan to AUTO.
  5. Fix leaks and keep sprinklers off the walls.
  6. Use a portable dehumidifier in problem rooms.

For whole-home control, a dehumidifier that connects to your HVAC system can keep every room in range automatically. Our indoor air quality team can check your humidity, airflow and AC sizing and recommend what fits your home.
faqs: What humidity level should my home be?

Somewhere between about 30 and 50 percent is comfortable for most people and discourages mold and dust mites. Coastal homes may run a bit higher at times, which is fine as long as you don't see condensation or mold.
Why is my house humid even with the AC running?
The most common reasons are an oversized system that short cycles, a fan left in the ON position, low airflow from a dirty filter or coil, and leaky return ducts pulling in damp air.
Is a whole-home dehumidifier worth it?
It can be for homes that stay damp despite ventilation fixes, especially near the coast or with a crawl space. It treats the whole house through your ducts instead of one room at a time.
Can high humidity cause mold in my HVAC system?
Yes. Moisture plus dust on coils, drain pans and ducts gives mold what it needs. Keeping humidity in range and the drain clear lowers that risk.
How Do You Keep Humidity Down in Your House?

Vent moisture out at the source with bathroom and kitchen fans, run your air conditioner, and use a dehumidifier where the house stays damp. Fix leaks, keep gutters and sprinklers away from the walls, and seal leaky ducts. Aim to keep indoor humidity between about 30 and 50 percent.
